The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on near-term economic activity and pose clear downside risks, but the FOMC’s rapid move to the effective lower bound, large-scale Treasury and agency MBS purchases, expanded repo operations, discount-window easing, and dollar swap lines are consistent with the credit channel and financial accelerator literature (e.g., Oliner and Rudebusch 1996a; Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein 1994; Gertler and Gilchrist 1994), which finds that easing financial frictions can stabilize cash flow, lower external finance premia, and support investment—especially for more constrained firms. Declines in market-based inflation compensation alongside little change in longer-term survey expectations suggest inflation expectations remain anchored, aligning with inflation-forecast-targeting insights (Svensson) and mitigating inflationary bias under discretion. Compared with historical episodes where delayed policy responses proved costly, swift action and clear commitment to maximum employment and price stability are likely to cushion the downturn. Net assessment: negative because of the shock and energy-sector stress, but less negative given credible and targeted policy support.
